title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport
whyNow: I want to understand how to do deep work, execute it, have it in my daily workflow, be it learning, reading, building products, working, exercise
questions: How does the deep work become in AI era, where working as deep work individual, and another person orchestrating AI to do the Deep Work?
What is advice for software engineer, who want to become tech lead -> senior software engineer-> CTO -> CEO -> Founder.

I am a perfectionist, I waste a lots of time perfecting, planning, rather than executing, iterating. My Deep work is mostiy perfecting, planning, making strategies, rather than executing, this slows down me. But on next thought, I think I can do the top level orchestration, planning, making strategies, and AI will do the execution

outsideView.replication: Not an empirical research program. Its main empirical anchor is Sophie Leroy's 2009 attention-residue study — real, but a single lab, one task-switching paradigm, since extended (Leroy & Glomb, 2018) rather than independently replicated at scale. Not on the standing failed-replication list, but the book leans on it more heavily than a single study supports.
outsideView.critics: The recurring, independent objection across multiple reviews: Newport writes from a tenured academic's unusual control over his own schedule, and prescriptions like blocking four uninterrupted hours don't obviously transfer to work structured around other people's availability — collaborative, hourly, or caregiving-constrained roles.
outsideView.agedBadly: Chapter 6's method for social media — a rational per-platform cost/benefit calculation — assumes tools chosen for a clear benefit. Newport has since said this doesn't match engagement-optimized platforms like TikTok, and has written that the underlying attention problem has gotten worse, not better, since 2016.

parts.title: The idea
parts.outcome: Explain, in your own words, why deep work is worth prioritizing and what specifically works against you doing it.

parts.title: The rules
parts.outcome: Run a concrete system — a scheduling philosophy, a boredom-tolerance practice, a tool-selection rule and a shallow-work budget — that turns the belief into actual deep work sessions.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Valuable
chapters.argues: The two abilities that make a knowledge worker valuable today — quickly mastering hard things and producing at an elite level — both depend on the capacity for deep work.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Rare
chapters.argues: Even though depth is valuable, modern knowledge-work culture — open offices, constant connectivity, an 'any benefit' approach to new tools — is structurally organized against it, because busyness substitutes for a real measure of productivity that most knowledge work lacks.

chapters.title: Deep Work Is Meaningful
chapters.argues: Beyond its economic payoff, deep work produces a felt sense of meaning — through flow and a craftsman's relationship to a skill — that shallow busyness structurally cannot.

chapters.title: Rule #1: Work Deeply
chapters.argues: Depth cannot be produced by willpower in the moment; it requires choosing in advance a scheduling philosophy and a set of rituals that remove the decision of whether and how to go deep from the moment itself.

chapters.title: Rule #2: Embrace Boredom
chapters.argues: The capacity to concentrate is trainable and also erodible: habitually reaching for stimulation the moment a task gets effortful teaches your brain to expect novelty, which undermines your ability to concentrate even when you intend to.

chapters.title: Rule #3: Quit Social Media
chapters.argues: Tools should be judged by whether they provide substantial net benefit to things you actually value, not by whether they provide any benefit at all — and by that stricter test, most people's social media use fails.

chapters.title: Rule #4: Drain the Shallows
chapters.argues: Shallow work cannot be eliminated, but it can and must be deliberately budgeted and minimized, because any hour not claimed in advance for something deep will default to something shallow.

exitCondition: Five consecutive weeks in which, across at least three of the domains you named — skill learning, reading, exercise, building, work — a scheduled deep work block was actually run on at least 4 of that week's scheduled days, with no week during that streak dropping to zero in any of the three domains.
